summary: Defines the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS), a method for turning JSON data into a single invariant representation so hashing and signing give repeatable results. The data can travel in its original form while operations run on the canonical form.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people can write the same story with different spacing. JCS rewrites it in one agreed way so everyone gets the same fingerprint.

questions: how do i sign json consistently
why does json property order matter
subtitle: Turn JSON data into an invariant form for reliable hashing and signing.

tldr.problem: JSON data can be written in many equivalent ways (different spacing, different property order) that look identical to humans but have different digital signatures and hashes.
tldr.mechanism: JCS defines a single canonical form for JSON: no extra whitespace, properties in alphabetical order, and numbers serialized using ECMAScript rules. Any JSON data canonicalized this way produces the same bytes.
tldr.outcome: Cryptographic operations on JSON data now work reliably across systems and organizations. A signed JSON object can remain JSON throughout its lifetime instead of being converted to base64.

today: RFC 8785 is an Informational RFC and is not an Internet Standard. It is used by JSON Web Key Thumbprint and compatible implementations exist in JavaScript, Java, Go, .NET, and Python.

sections.title: Why JSON Needs a Canonical Form
sections.content:
JSON is text data in a format that computers can parse. But the same data can be written in many ways: {"a":1,"b":2} and {"b": 2, "a": 1} mean the same thing to a parser, though they are different sequences of bytes. This matters for cryptography. When you sign or hash data, you are computing a fingerprint of the exact bytes. If the bytes change, even just the order or spacing, the fingerprint changes. Two computers cannot verify the same signature on the same data if they write it differently.

JCS solves this by defining the one true way to write any JSON data. It is based on rules from ECMAScript (JavaScript), which is a widely-used language with consistent number and string formatting. If two systems both canonicalize before signing, their signatures will match.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine signing a contract. If one person writes it with different word order or spacing, both versions might say the same thing, but the signatures won't match. JCS is the rule that says: rewrite it this exact way first, then sign it.

sections.title: How Canonicalization Works
sections.content:
Whitespace removal: All spaces, newlines, and indentation are removed from the output.

Number serialization: Every number is written using the ECMAScript rule. For example, 4.50 becomes 4.5, and 1E30 becomes 1e+30. This ensures that equivalent numbers are written identically.

String escaping: Control characters in strings are escaped using lowercase hex, like \u000f. Regular characters stay as-is unless they are backslash or quote, which are escaped as \\ and \".

Property sorting: In JSON objects, properties are sorted alphabetically by their name (treating the name as a string of UTF-16 code units, not by language rules). Arrays keep their original order.

UTF-8 encoding: The final output is encoded in UTF-8 bytes, which is platform-independent.
sections.plainLanguage: The four steps are: squeeze out all spacing, write numbers in one agreed way, sort the labels alphabetically, and encode into bytes everyone uses.

sections.title: Using JCS for Signing and Hashing
sections.content:
The data to be signed is an I-JSON object, which is a subset of JSON. It must have no duplicate property names, strings that are valid Unicode, and numbers that fit in IEEE 754 double-precision (a standard 64-bit float). If a number does not fit (like a huge integer or a bank amount), wrap it as a JSON string and handle the conversion at the application layer.

To sign with JCS: (1) serialize the data as JSON using standard tools, (2) pass the result through a JCS canonicalizer, which outputs UTF-8 bytes, (3) sign those bytes with your cryptographic key. To verify: (1) parse the signed JSON, (2) read and save the signature, (3) remove the signature property from the object, (4) canonicalize the remaining object, (5) verify the signature against the canonical bytes.

One key advantage: the original JSON document can carry the signature as a property and remain valid JSON. You do not have to convert it to base64 or wrap it in another format.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign: canonicalize the data to get the fingerprint bytes, then sign the bytes. To verify: strip the signature, canonicalize again, and check that the signature matches the new fingerprint.

sections.title: Why This Design Matters
sections.content:
JCS builds on ECMAScript serialization, which is already implemented in JavaScript engines, Java, .NET, and Node.js. This avoids reinventing a new rule set and makes implementations simpler. It is also compatible with existing JSON tools: you do not need a special JSON parser, just a post-processing canonicalizer.

It is more robust than prior XML canonicalization standards, which suffered from complexity and interoperability issues. JSON has no namespaces or default values, so its canonicalization is much simpler. JCS is already used by JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint and systems like Keybase.

For applications handling very large numbers (beyond IEEE 754 precision), the RFC describes how to represent them as JSON strings and still sign consistently. The document also notes that Unicode normalization is not applied: strings are canonicalized as-is.
sections.plainLanguage: JCS is simple because JSON is simpler than XML. It reuses existing JavaScript rules that most programmers already know. And it works with the JSON tools you already have.
